name: Log returns
brief:
Simple returns do not add up over time. A fall of 0.5 then a rise of 1.0 leaves you where you started, yet they sum to 0.5. Log returns fix that, so researchers use them to add returns across days.

Write `log_returns(prices)`. It takes closing prices in time order and returns one log return for each day after the first.
definition:
The log return on day $t$ is the natural log of the price ratio:

$$\ell_t = \ln \dfrac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}$$

They add up: $\ell_1 + \dots + \ell_n = \ln \tfrac{P_n}{P_0}$. Return an empty list for fewer than two prices. Every price is positive.
constraints: $O(n)$ time, where $n$ is the number of prices.
Use the `math` module. NumPy is not loaded.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Import `math` at the top. Pair each price with the one before it and take `math.log` of today over yesterday.

examples.note: $\ln \tfrac{110}{100} = \ln 1.1 \approx 0.0953$, a little below the simple return of 0.1.
Down by half, then back. The two log returns cancel exactly.

tests.name: Empty list
tests.why: With no prices there are no returns. Return an empty list.

tests.name: Single price
tests.why: One price has nothing before it, so there are no returns yet.

tests.name: Flat prices
tests.why: A price that does not move has a log return of $\ln 1 = 0$.

tests.name: Doubling
tests.why: Each doubling is $\ln 2 \approx 0.693$. Log returns of equal moves are equal.

tests.name: Natural log
tests.why: `math.log10` gives 1.0 here. Returns use the natural log, `math.log`, so the answer is $\ln 10$.

tests.name: Ratio, not difference
tests.why: Take the log of today over yesterday, not of the price difference.

tests.name: Daily closes
tests.why: Return one log return for each day after the first, in order, without rounding.

tests.name: They add up
tests.note: The sum of your log returns
tests.why: The log returns should sum to $\ln(98.6 / 101.25)$. Check you used the natural log of each ratio.

tests.name: Long series
tests.note: 100,000 prices from a seeded random walk; the last three returns are checked
tests.why: This test has 100,000 prices. Check that you return one value per day after the first, in order.

how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests, including one that sums your returns. Lists are compared element by element, and each float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value.
where: Part of the 1.1 exit project: returns, annualised volatility and maximum drawdown from a CSV of daily prices.
notes: `math.log` with one argument is the natural log, base $e$.
`zip(prices, prices[1:])` gives each (yesterday, today) pair once.
Summing the result gives $\ln(P_n / P_0)$, the log of the total move.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out
